title: Today You Are A Man

jokes.text: Liz receives a package and immediately announces 'My trio of popcorns' — a non-sequitur reveal that she was anticipating bulk snack delivery at work
jokes.setup: A package arrives for Liz at work
jokes.punchline: She immediately identifies it as 'My trio of popcorns' — the specific absurdity of ordering a trio of popcorns and awaiting it eagerly at work
jokes.explanation: Perfect Liz Lemon character shorthand — her excitement about bulk snack delivery at the office tells us everything about her. High economy: three words do heavy lifting. Strong character integration because this is specifically Liz.

jokes.text: Kenneth asks if they missed him while he was gone; Jenna says she saw him yesterday and he was 'in the kitchen all day' — but it was a broom
jokes.setup: Kenneth points out he was fired for the day; Jenna insists she saw him
jokes.punchline: She was looking at a broom the whole time and didn't notice the difference
jokes.explanation: The payoff ('Oh, that's a broom') is a clean, well-timed visual comedy beat. Jenna being so self-absorbed she didn't notice her colleague was replaced by a broom is perfect character integration. Good structure with a clean pivot.

jokes.text: Kenneth uses his 'once-in-a-lifetime interruption' to argue he is not even a dog to them, then pivots to: 'when a dog goes missing, everyone's upset 'cause there's no dog milk for the babies'
jokes.setup: Kenneth makes a heartfelt speech about wanting to be valued like a pet
jokes.punchline: The logic collapses into the absurdist non-sequitur that dogs produce milk for human babies — delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: This joke works on multiple levels: the formality of 'once-in-a-lifetime interruption' is a Kenneth-specific absurdism, then the emotional pitch of the speech collapses into the bizarre rural logic about dog milk for babies. Extremely high character integration — this is pure Kenneth Parcell. The 'dog milk for babies' is genuinely strange and original. Justifies the 8+ rating.

jokes.text: Liz says she has a 'bone to pick' with Jack; Jack ignores her entirely and pivots immediately to talking about the Pentagon weaponizing microwave technology
jokes.setup: Liz walks in with an agenda ('I have a bone to pick with you')
jokes.punchline: Jack doesn't acknowledge her at all and launches into his own monologue about GE and the Pentagon — her concerns are irrelevant
jokes.explanation: A reliable Jack/Liz dynamic joke — his dismissiveness of her concerns while pursuing his own grandiose preoccupations. Functional and character-specific but not particularly novel within the show's vocabulary.

jokes.text: Liz's contract demands include 'a hospital bed in my office. A real one. I don't care if it's against the law to resell them.'
jokes.setup: Jack asks what Liz even wants in a renegotiation
jokes.punchline: Her primary demand is an illegally resold hospital bed for her office — the specificity of knowing the resale is illegal implies she's already researched it
jokes.explanation: The kicker 'I don't care if it's against the law to resell them' implies Liz has already looked into this and been told it's a problem — her obsessive comfort-seeking has crossed into legal research. Excellent character integration for Liz's sloth and weirdness.

jokes.text: Jack's nostalgic flashback shows him closing a deal with the line 'So it's agreed. You'll be moving forward with this partnership' — presented as legendary dealmaking prowess
jokes.setup: Jack says 'When there was a deal no one could close, they brought in Donaghy' — building up to legendary negotiating
jokes.punchline: The 'legendary' closing line is completely mundane corporate speak — the gap between his self-mythology and reality
jokes.explanation: The subversion of Jack's self-mythology with a completely ordinary corporate phrase works adequately. The irony is clear but the execution isn't sharp enough to be memorable.

jokes.text: Liz tells Jack to call her assistant to set up a meeting; Jack immediately says 'And by your assistant, you mean you with a British accent?' — Liz confirms she has a new assistant from South Africa; Jack says 'Yeah, she'll be British'
jokes.setup: Liz says to call her assistant; Jack assumes she doesn't have one
jokes.punchline: Liz's new assistant is from South Africa; Jack dismisses this with 'Yeah, she'll be British' — implying he'll just ignore the distinction
jokes.explanation: A two-stage joke: first the assumption that Liz is her own assistant (good character beat), then the dismissive 'she'll be British' punchline which is economical and captures Jack's casual imperialism. The second beat is the stronger one.

jokes.text: Tracy asks 'Now Marty, how Jewish is everyone here? 'Cause I may need to change parts of my act.'
jokes.setup: Tracy and Jenna are about to perform at a Bar Mitzvah
jokes.punchline: Tracy asks for a Jewish-ness calibration before performing, implying his act has antisemitic content he'd edit for the room — and that he does this routinely
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Tracy asking for audience composition data before modifying offensive material implies this is standard professional practice for him — and that there's a sliding scale. Pure Tracy Jordan character comedy.

jokes.text: Adam says he loved TGS; Marty says 'I was being sarcastic. God, I told mom I wanted Transformer's theme for Bar Mitzvah. You know, this sucks. I hate you.' — directed at his father
jokes.setup: Marty presents Tracy and Jenna as a surprise for his son who 'loves TGS'
jokes.punchline: Adam reveals he was lying, hates TGS, wanted Transformers, and immediately goes into full teenager mode
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy — the Bar Mitzvah kid's brutal honesty sets up the episode's conflict. The 'I was being sarcastic' reversal works but isn't particularly novel.

jokes.text: Pete's strategy for handling Kenneth's 'tantrum': 'When your kid throws a tantrum and holds his breath, you hold your breath too. When you regain consciousness, believe me, he's ready to leave the toy store.'
jokes.setup: The staff debates how to handle Kenneth withholding his services to make them beg
jokes.punchline: Pete's parenting 'wisdom' involves passing out from holding your breath until your child complies — an insane and dangerous strategy delivered as sage advice
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup is conventional parenting wisdom framing, then the logic leads to Pete passing out in a toy store — and the kicker ('when you regain consciousness, believe me, he's ready to leave') implies this has worked. The confidence of the delivery is everything. High originality (the passing-out detail is not a predictable beat), perfect structure. Justifies 8+ clearly.

jokes.text: Jack accuses Liz of being coached — 'Is it Pat Riley? Tell him the Funmeister says hi. He'll know what that means.'
jokes.setup: Jack is surprised by Liz's negotiating skill and suspects she has a coach
jokes.punchline: He suspects Pat Riley and has a specific, mysterious nickname ('the Funmeister') that Riley would supposedly recognize
jokes.explanation: The implication that Jack has a secret nickname with Pat Riley — 'the Funmeister' — is wonderfully absurd. The confidence with which he sends the message ('he'll know what that means') suggests a whole shadow world of Jack's relationships with powerful men. Good character integration.

jokes.text: No one has ever won a land war in Russia — 'Not Napoleon, not Hitler, not even Balki in the unaired ninth season of Perfect Strangers'
jokes.setup: Jack explains the concept of 'home turf' in negotiation, using historical examples
jokes.punchline: After Napoleon and Hitler, the third example is Balki from Perfect Strangers — a fictional character from a cancelled sitcom — and the specific detail that the ninth season was unaired
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The escalation from real historical atrocities (Napoleon, Hitler) to a sitcom character (Balki from Perfect Strangers) is a perfect comedic left-turn. Then the 'unaired ninth season' adds fictional specificity — as if this season exists in Jack's mythology. The confidence of including Balki alongside Napoleon and Hitler is the genius move. One of 30 Rock's signature move: absurd specificity in a list. Justifies 8+ easily.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Jack Donaghy...playing with himself.' Beat. 'It's a Jack-off.'
jokes.setup: Jack relishes the idea of negotiating against himself as 'the ultimate game'
jokes.punchline: The double entendre: 'playing with himself' → 'It's a Jack-off' (both a pun on his name and a euphemism)
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed dirty pun that works better than most because the show commits fully to it. The beat between 'playing with himself' and 'It's a Jack-off' is timed well. It's still fundamentally a crude pun, which limits the craft ceiling, but it's executed cleanly.

jokes.text: Jenna tells Tracy that their Bar Mitzvah performance was 'that pathetic butchering of Who's on first?' — Tracy responds: 'Who's on first! That's the phrase I couldn't remember.'
jokes.setup: Jenna scolds Tracy for their bad Abbott & Costello attempt
jokes.punchline: Tracy didn't know the name of the routine he was doing — 'That's the phrase I couldn't remember' — implying he tried to perform it without knowing its name
jokes.explanation: Good Tracy moment — his obliviousness about the routine he was performing poorly is consistent with his character. The punchline lands because it reframes the earlier failure retroactively.

jokes.text: Liz's 'home turf' — the place she cannot lose — turns out to be an ice cream store
jokes.setup: Jack's video asks 'What is your home turf? The one place in the world where you cannot lose'
jokes.punchline: Cut to: an ice cream store. Liz's ultimate power base is an ice cream shop
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — we don't need to see Liz choose this, we just cut there. The negotiation happening in an ice cream store as Liz's 'power home turf' is both absurd and perfectly consistent with her character. The visual setup of this meeting at Jack's eventual height disadvantage pays off the video's lesson in the best possible way. Near-perfect character integration. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Tracy suggests that he and Jenna should be honest at work, 'Like the polio vaccine. Or a no-bottom strip club near a Wendy's.'
jokes.setup: Tracy agrees to be honest about feelings going forward — the comparison to positive things in the world
jokes.punchline: The second example of 'a good thing in the world' is 'a no-bottom strip club near a Wendy's' — which Tracy considers equivalent to the polio vaccine
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: (1) 'no-bottom' strip club is a wonderfully specific type of establishment to imagine, (2) 'near a Wendy's' adds a crucial detail of convenience dining that makes Tracy's ideal world vivid. The casual equivalence with the polio vaccine is the perfect frame. This is uniquely Tracy Jordan — his utopia is a late-night strip club/burger combo. High quotability, high character integration. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Liz counters Jack's 'sorcerer's apprentice' with 'a pirate holiday,' forcing Jack to 'play the hillbilly auction' — all negotiation tactics from Jack's tapes
jokes.setup: The negotiation has escalated to named tactics from Jack's playbook
jokes.punchline: The ridiculous names of negotiating gambits ('sorcerer's apprentice,' 'pirate holiday,' 'hillbilly auction') presented as formal techniques
jokes.explanation: The absurd nomenclature of Jack's negotiation gambits — each name more outlandish than the last — is a signature 30 Rock move: inventing specific-sounding jargon for made-up systems. The 'hillbilly auction' in particular is a great nonsense phrase.

jokes.text: Jack's spiral: 'I used to be a winner. Men wanted to be me, women wanted to sleep with me, bisexuals wanted to watch.'
jokes.setup: Jack is spiraling after losing the negotiation
jokes.punchline: The escalating desire-sequence ends with 'bisexuals wanted to watch' — completing the spectrum with a surprisingly specific and inclusive third category
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and among 30 Rock's most quotable lines. The classic 'men wanted to be me, women wanted to sleep with me' is a stock phrase, but the addition of 'bisexuals wanted to watch' as a third category is unexpected, inclusive in an absurd way, and perfectly escalates the list. The structure is impeccable — two expected beats, one perfect subversion. 'Watch' is the ideal word choice. High economy (the joke is 17 words). Justifies 8+ with complete confidence.

jokes.text: Jack's breakdown fantasy alternative: quitting to work at a not-for-profit, 'where there's less pressure and the people are nice. And I can wear sneakers and jeans on Friday.'
jokes.setup: Jack is spiraling and threatens to quit everything
jokes.punchline: His imagined utopia — Casual Friday — is the most pathetic possible aspiration for a man of his power, and he says it with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The gap between Jack's usual world-dominating aspirations and his imagined utopia of 'sneakers and jeans on Friday' is the joke — and the escalating spiral that gets there through 'less pressure' and 'people are nice' makes it land harder. Jack's idea of rock-bottom is Casual Friday.

tmdb_overview: Liz finds a secret weapon to help in her contract negotiations with Jack, Kenneth leaves his job because he feels under-appreciated, and Tracy and Jenna perform at their accountant's ungrateful son's Bar Mitzvah.
insight: Bar mitzvah subplot drives 72 jokes across 30 minutes with escalating absurdist chaos.
